Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology of pediatric musculoskeletal malignancies.
Perform an appropriate diagnostic workup for of pediatric musculoskeletal malignancies.
Apply appropriate treatment principles for pediatric patients with musculoskeletal malignancy.

Benign bone lesions are more common than malignant lesions in children, which may
delay the diagnosis. Although benign bone lesions often are incidental findings,
malignant lesions usually present as pain. Night pain usually is a late finding, and a high
index of suspicion is essential if surgeons encounter a patient with pain out of
proportion to radiographic findings or with an atypical presentation. Osteosarcomas are
the most frequent malignant bone tumors in the pediatric population followed by Ewing
sarcoma (EWS). Bones also may be involved in systemic malignancies, such as leukemia
and lymphoma, or in metastatic processes, such as metastatic neuroblastoma.

Diagnostic Workup
Clinical Evaluation

Clinical Evaluation
The clinical evaluation includes a thorough patient history and physical examination.
Most patients with a malignant bone tumor initially present with pain, which may be
aggravated by activity; however, this may progress to pain at rest and night pain. EWS
may masquerade as infection, and children with EWS may have pain, fever, swelling, and
increased inflammatory markers, which may result in a misdiagnosis of osteomyelitis. A
rapidly increasing mass should increase suspicion for a malignant process. Systemic
symptoms, such as fever and drenching night sweats may be noted in patients with
lymphoma. Physical examination helps determine the extent of soft-tissue involvement,
proximity, and function of adjacent neurovascular structures and joints. Reactive
effusions may be observed in adjacent joints and should be differentiated from
infiltration of the joint by the tumor. Regional lymph node involvement is rarely observed
in patients with osteosarcoma or EWS but may be present in patients with lymphoma or
leukemia. A baseline measure of limb lengths may be essential before planning a
reconstructive procedure.
Imaging Studies
Imaging is the cornerstone of the diagnostic workup in most patients. This consists of various
imaging modalities.

Plain Radiography
Plain radiography often is the most useful diagnostic imaging modality in patients with a bone
tumor but is of limited value in patients with a soft-tissue tumor.
Radiography helps to establish a differential diagnosis, suggests the biology of the tumor, and
may be diagnostic in many patients.
The anatomic location of the lesion (eg, the bone and the part of the bone), the zone of
transition, the mineralization pattern, periosteal reaction, and the presence or absence of a
soft-tissue extension should be evaluated.
The Codman triangle (angle) is the new bone formation at the junction between the cortex and
the elevated periosteum. This may be observed in any tumor with soft-tissue extension that
elevates the periosteum.
The spiculated (sunburst) periosteal response may be observed in osteosarcoma, and a
lamellated (onion skin) response may be observed in EWS; however, these responses are not
exclusive to the respective diagnoses and are not diagnostic.
Radiographs may reveal eccentric calcification of variable degree in patients with synovial
sarcoma. The pattern of mineralization may help differentiate synovial sarcoma from
heterotopic ossification.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI has become standard imaging modality for the diagnosis and evaluation of the local
extent of most bone and soft-tissue lesions (with the notable exception of osteoid osteomas,
which are better evaluated via fine-cut CT).
MRI also aids in detecting skip metastases in patients with osteosarcoma; therefore, imaging
the entire length of the affected bone is essential.
Computed Tomography
CT of the chest is included in the staging workup to diagnose lung metastases in patients with
osteosarcoma and patients with EWS.
CT of the abdomen and pelvis is not routinely recommended.

Bone scintigraphy is essential for staging malignant bone lesions (such as osteosarcoma and
EWS) and for evaluating metastatic disease.
The role of positron emission tomography (PET) continues to evolve and has become standard
in the staging of lymphomas and melanomas (in adults).
PET scans are being used with increasing frequency to stage other tumors and predict the
response to chemotherapy (potentially guiding the selection of proper margins of resection).
Biopsy

Biopsy
This is the final step in the diagnostic workup of musculoskeletal tumors. Imaging studies
should be obtained before biopsy and may guide the planning of the biopsy. Biopsy
principles are outlined in Table 2.
Table 2 Principles of Biopsy of Bone and Soft-Tissue Tumors
The biopsy should be performed at the site of definitive management if possible.
Review clinical and radiographic findings with a radiologist and pathologist before
biopsy.
Use a tourniquet but avoid expressive exsanguination (Esmarch bandage).
Use the shortest possible incision, longitudinally placed, along the line of definitive
resection.
Minimize soft-tissue dissection and contamination by dissecting through muscle,
taking the most direct route feasible to the tumor.
Biopsy the advancing edge of the tumor, obtaining adequate lesional tissue (frozen
section).
Obtain good hemostasis before closure with the use of a drain (brought out in line
with the incision) as necessary.
Sutures should be placed close to the skin edge to minimize the amount of skin to be
excised at definitive resection.

Osteosarcoma
Introduction
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary sarcoma of bone in children.
The most common malignancy in bone in adults is metastatic disease, and the most common
primary bone malignancy in adults is myeloma.

Predisposing Syndromes
Predisposing syndromes include Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 pathway), congenital
retinoblastoma (RB1 gene pathway), and Rothmund-Thompson syndrome, among others.
Patient Age
Age distribution is bimodal, with an earlier and larger peak occurring in and around the
adolescent growth spurt and a second peak occurring in older adults with Paget disease or a
history of radiation therapy.
Sites
Osteosarcoma is most common in the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.
Axial involvement is more common in secondary osteosarcomas.
Approximately 10% to 20% of patients present with metastatic disease (poor prognostic
factor). The most common sites for metastasis include the lungs and bone.
Clinical Features
Clinical features include pain, swelling, and pressure effect on surrounding structures.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs demonstrate a sclerotic or mixed lucent and sclerotic, poorly marginated lesion,
usually involving the metaphysis of the long bone.
Extension into the surrounding soft tissues (soft-tissue mass) is commonly observed on
presentation (extracompartmental high-grade lesion).
A Codman triangle and sunburst/speculated periosteal reaction may be observed.
The physis is not a good barrier to spread; if extensive physeal abutment of the tumor is
present, extension into the epiphysis is likely.
MRI of the entire extent of the bone may reveal skip lesions in 3% to 5% of patients.
Skip Lesions
Skip lesions are lesions that are discontinuous from the primary lesion (separated from it by
normal marrow) within the same bone.

Patients with skip lesions are thought to have a poorer prognosis; however, if the lesions are
adequately resected, patients have outcomes similar to those of patients without skip lesions.1
Staging Workup
The staging workup includes MRI of the full length of the bone involved (to assess for skip
lesions and local extent), chest CT (the lungs are the most common site of metastatic disease),
and full-body bone scintigraphy or PET (bones are the second most common sites of
metastatic disease).
Pathology

Pathology
The histologic hallmark of osteosarcoma is production of malignant osteoid by the
tumor cells. Various histologic subtypes exist. Conventional/intramedullary high-grade
osteosarcoma can be histologically subdivided into osteoblastic, chondroblastic,
fibroblastic, and telangiectatic subtypes. A low-grade central osteosarcoma variant may
be misdiagnosed as fibrous dysplasia, desmoplastic fibroma, or other conditions. This
may recur as a high-grade tumor after inadequate management. Surface osteosarcomas
can be subdivided into periosteal osteosarcoma, parosteal osteosarcoma, and high-
grade surface osteosarcoma. Other rare variants include small cell osteosarcoma and
giant cell-rich osteosarcoma.
Periosteal Osteosarcoma
Periosteal osteosarcoma usually is an intermediate-grade surface/juxtacortical osteosarcoma
with a propensity for the diaphysis of the femur or tibia.
Imaging studies typically reveal a broad-based surface soft-tissue mass causing extrinsic
erosion of thickened underlying diaphyseal cortex and perpendicular periosteal reaction
extending into the soft-tissue component of the lesion.
Histologically, the lesion usually is chondroblastic.

Management involves wide surgical excision, and the role of chemotherapy remains
controversial.
The 10-year survival rate is 80% to 90%.2
Parosteal Osteosarcoma
This low-grade surface tumor typically presents as a stuck-on appearance on the cortex of the
underlying bone.
Marrow involvement may be observed in approximately one-third of patients.
Histologically, these lesions are mostly fibrous; however, they can de-differentiate.
Management involves wide excision alone; and patients do not require chemotherapy.
Survival is excellent with adequate local control. De-differentiated tumors are associated with
a poorer prognosis.3,4
Management of Conventional Osteosarcoma
Chemotherapy has improved the 5-year survival rates of patients with osteosarcoma from 10%
to 15% with surgical treatment alone to higher than 70% in patients with nonmetastatic
disease on presentation. Chemotherapy in patients with osteosarcoma typically consists of a
multidrug regimen (most commonly cisplatin, doxorubicin, and high-dose methotrexate
administered as two cycles preoperatively/in a neoadjuvant fashion and as four cycles
postoperatively/in an adjuvant fashion).
Surgical resection with wide margins (cuff of normal tissue) with an attempt to preserve
function is the preferred surgical treatment strategy. Surgical management usually is
performed after two cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy have been completed and the
staging workup has been repeated. Surgical management may involve limb salvage, which is
achievable in 80% to 85% of patients, or amputation followed by prosthetic fitting. van Nes
rotationplasty and/or tibial turn-up are methods of functional amputation with improved
prosthetic function. Surgical management also can be offered for resection of metastatic
lesions (especially in the lungs).
Radiation therapy has a limited role in the management of osteosarcoma.
Recurrence

The rate of local recurrence postoperatively is 5% to 10%. Risk factors include pathologic
fracture, poor response to chemotherapy, and inadequate margins. Most osteosarcomas
(80%) recur in the soft tissues rather than in bone (20%). Prognosis is poorer if local recurrence
occurs (40% 5-year survival rate).5 A high risk of metastatic disease concurrently or
subsequently to a local recurrence also exists, leading to a poorer overall prognosis.
Approximately 5% to 10% of patients with osteosarcoma experience a pathologic fracture on
presentation or during treatment. Approximately two-thirds are nondisplaced, and as many as
one-fourth will have positive surgical margins. The local recurrence rate after limb salvage for a
pathologic fracture (with negative margins) in appropriately selected patients is not higher
than that in patients undergoing an amputation; however, the 5-year survival rate is slightly
poorer (50% versus 66%, respectively, in a systematic review by Salunke et al).6
Prognosis
The 5-year overall survival rate of patients with nonmetastatic osteosarcoma is approximately
70%. This decreases to approximately 20% in patients with metastatic disease or skip lesions
(two foci of tumor in the same bone with a normal segment in between). Patients with lung-
only metastasis have better (approximately 40%) 5-year survival compared with patients with
bone, soft-tissue, or node metastases.
Prognostic factors include stage at presentation (size, tumor biology, metastatic disease),
location (determines ability to attain negative margins), alkaline phosphatase level at
presentation (more than three times normal is associated with poorer prognosis), surgical
margins, response to chemotherapy (greater than 90% tumor necrosis is considered a good
response; fibroblastic and telangiectatic respond better; chondroblastic respond poorer), and
the presence of pathologic fractures.7
Ewing Sarcoma
Introduction
EWS, originally described by James Ewing in 1921, is the second most common bone sarcoma
in the pediatric population. It accounts for approximately 2% of pediatric cancers. The Ewing
family of tumors, which share the same chromosomal translocation, consists of EWS of bone,
extraosseous EWS, primitive neuroectodermal tumor, and Askin tumor (of the chest wall).

Genetics
EWS usually is associated with a characteristic t(11;22)(11q24-22q12) translocation, with an
EWS-FLI1 fusion transcript. This fusion transcript codes for an abnormal protein that is involved
in the pathogenesis of EWS (exact mechanism is not well defined). This is observed in
approximately 85% to 90% of patients with EWS. In the remaining patients, EWS may fuse with
a gene other than a FLI1 gene, usually from the ETS family, with the ETS-related gene being the
next most common gene.8
Patient Age
EWS is commonly observed in adolescents.
Most patients are diagnosed from age 0 to 20 years, with the median age being 15 years.
EWS is three times as common as osteosarcoma in individuals aged 0 to 10 years and becomes
less common in individuals aged 11 to 20 years.
EWS has been described in children as early as age 1.
Sites
The most common sites of involvement include the lower extremity (approximately 40% of
patients), pelvis (approximately 25%), and upper extremity (10%).
Spine involvement may be observed in approximately 5% to 6% patients.
The most common sites are the distal femur, proximal femur, and pelvis.
Axial skeletal involvement is more common in patients with EWS than patients with
osteosarcoma, particularly in the pelvis.
Diaphyseal involvement is frequent (approximately 50%) but by no means exclusive.
Soft-tissue extension often is observed and may be quite large.
Lung and bone marrow are the most common sites of distant metastatic disease.
Patients with extraosseous EWS are more likely to be older, be female, be nonwhite, and have
axial primary sites; however, they are less likely to have pelvic primary sites than patients with
skeletal EWS, according to a survey of the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results
database.9
Clinical Features

The most common patient age is 11 to 20 years (median age, 15 years), and boys are affected
more frequently than girls.
EWS is most frequently observed in the Caucasian population, with involvement in African
Americans being quite rare. Occurrence in Asians is somewhat more common than in African
Americans but far less so than in Caucasians.10
The presenting features may include pain, swelling, and occasionally fever and tiredness.
EWS may be mistaken for an infection (culture every biopsy and biopsy every culture).
Symptoms also may originate from compression of local structures, including the spinal cord
in patients with spine involvement.
Metastatic lung involvement may present as shortness of breath and pleural effusions.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
No obvious osseous destruction may be noted in the early part of the disease process.
Given the aggressive nature of the tumor, a permeative appearance may be noted as the
tumor erodes through the bone cortex.
Soft-tissue involvement may be observed early in the disease process, and a lamellated (onion
skin) periosteal reaction may be noted.
Note that all lamellated periosteal reactions do not indicate a diagnosis of EWS, and not all
patients with EWS have a lamellated periosteal response.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is very useful in determining the extent of involvement of the marrow and the soft tissue.
Often, in the pelvis, soft-tissue involvement may be observed beyond the inner and the outer
tables.
MRI after neoadjuvant chemotherapy often reveals considerable shrinkage of the soft-tissue
component of the tumor because it is chemosensitive.
Computed Tomography
CT of the chest is performed for initial staging, for restaging before definitive local
management, and for surveillance.

Staging Workup
Local staging includes radiographs and MRI of the involved bone.
Distant staging, similar to that for osteosarcomas, includes CT of the chest and full-body bone
scintigraphy. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose–PET with or without CT or MRI may be performed in lieu
of bone scintigraphy.
Additional staging specific to EWS includes a bone marrow biopsy to assess for bone marrow
metastases.
The role of routine bone marrow sampling recently has been questioned given the low
prevalence of bone marrow-only metastases; however, it remains the standard of care.11
No role exists for routine CT of the abdomen and pelvis in the staging of EWS.
Staging is performed at the time of diagnosis, and the workup often is repeated before
definitive local management.
Pathology
Histologically, EWS consists of small, round blue cells, which are uniform and have scant
cytoplasm and indistinct cell membranes.
The nuclei are round and indented and amphophilic.
The cells are in sheets divided into irregular lobules by fibrous strands. They may be arranged
in pseudorosettes rather than rosettes around neurofibrillary cores (Homer-Wright rosettes)
or central lumina (Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes), as observed in primitive neuroectodermal
tumors.
Immunohistochemistry demonstrates diffuse vimentin staining and membranous staining with
cluster of differentiation 99 (not specific for EWS) and nuclear staining for FLI1 (more sensitive).
Cytogenetics using fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrates the characteristic 11:22
translocation in most patients or EWSR1 fusion with some of the other fusion partners in 10%
to 15% of patients (ETS-related gene on chromosome 21q22 is the next most common).
Management
The Ewing family of tumors are exquisitely chemosensitive and radiosensitive. Management
typically is multimodal.12
Management for nonmetastatic EWS typically involves chemotherapy (usually six cycles)
followed by local control and additional chemotherapy (total of approximately 15 cycles).

Chemotherapy regimens typically include vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and
alternating with ifosfamide and etoposide. Some regimens, mostly in Europe, include
dactinomycin.
Evidence suggest that vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide alternating with
ifosfamide and etoposide at 2-week intervals is associated with better event-free survival (EFS)
at 3-week intervals in patients with nonmetastatic EWS (73% versus 65%, respectively).
High-dose chemotherapy with busulfan and melphalan followed by stem cell transplantation
was shown to be beneficial in patients with poor tumor necrosis (<90%) with induction
chemotherapy or large tumors (>200 mL) in the Euro-EWING99 and Ewing-2008 study with less
intensive induction chemotherapy.13 This regimen is not beneficial in patients with metastatic
disease.
The role of irinotecan, topotecan, temozolomide, monoclonal antibodies, and immunotherapy
is being investigated.
Management
Radiation Therapy
Although EWS is radiosensitive, surgical management is the preferred form of local treatment.
Data do not show a clear difference in outcomes between patients undergoing radiation
therapy alone versus those undergoing surgical treatment of local control.14
Radiation therapy can be performed in a neoadjuvant fashion in patients in whom marginal
resection is anticipated. Radiation therapy may be performed postoperatively in patients with
a microscopically or grossly positive margin. Radiation therapy may be used for definitive local
control in patients in whom surgical treatment is not feasible or is unsafe.
The radiation therapy dose is approximately 50.4 Gy for patients with microscopically positive
margins, whereas the dose typically is 55.8 Gy (45 Gy at the time of local control and 10.8 Gy at
the end of chemotherapy) for patients undergoing radiation therapy as definitive treatment.
Risks of radiation therapy in the pediatric population include damage to growth plates and
growth abnormalities and a dose-dependent risk for a second malignancy (approximately 5%
in those receiving a radiation therapy dose of 48 to 60 Gy).15 In addition, the degree of tumor
necrosis cannot be calculated in patients receiving radiation therapy alone for local treatment.
Whole lung radiation therapy (12 to 15 Gy) should be considered in patients with lung
metastases, even if they resolve with induction chemotherapy.

Surgical Management
Excision of the tumor with wide margins is the preferred treatment option for local control
provided resection margins are adequate. In patients with unresectable tumors or in those in
whom surgical treatment would cause considerable functional or cosmetic problems, radiation
therapy may be used as the definitive local treatment option.
Emerging data from the Euro-EWING99 study suggest a survival benefit may be associated
with adjuvant radiation therapy, even in patients without metastasis in whom adequate
(negative) resection margins are achieved; however, selection criteria in this study were not
standardized.16
Timing of local control (radiation more so than surgery) affects 5- and 10-year overall survival,
with patients undergoing local control between 6 and 15 weeks having better outcomes (78.7%
and 70.3%, respectively) than those undergoing local control later (70.4% and 57.1%,
respectively).17
Prognosis
The prognosis in patients with EWS is influenced by several factors. Poor prognostic factors
include the following:
Age older than 18 years (children younger than 10 years tend to have better outcomes than
adolescents)
Boys have a poorer prognosis than girls.
The volume/size of tumors is more than 8 cm or 200 mL.
Tumors located in the pelvis and the axial skeleton are harder to resect with negative
margins. Extraskeletal tumors result in better outcomes than EWS of bone.
Elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels are present.
Circulating tumor DNA is detected in blood.
Metastatic disease on presentation indicates poorer prognosis.
Poor response to chemotherapy
The 5-year EFS and 5-year overall survival of patients with localized EWS in the Children’s
Oncology Group (COG)-AEWS1031 trial were 73% and 88%, respectively.11 The prognosis of
metastatic EWS is much poorer, with a 6-year EFS of 28% and overall survival of 30%.18
Patients with lung-only metastasis who undergo bilateral lung radiation therapy tend to have
better outcomes than those with bone marrow/bone metastasis. Patients with multifocal

Introduction
Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft-tissue sarcoma (STS) in the pediatric
population (50% of all soft-tissue malignancies).
It arises from the undifferentiated mesoderm and has phenotypic and biologic features of
primitive skeletal muscle.
It accounts for 3.5% of cancers in individuals younger than 15 years and approximately 2% of
cancers in those aged 15 to 19 years.
Approximately 350 new cases are diagnosed every year (incidence of 4.5 per 1 million
children). The most common type is embryonal RMS (four per 1 million children), followed by
alveolar RMS (one per 1 million children). The other variants (botryoid, pleomorphic, spindle
cell, etc.) are far less common.20
Genetics
Embryonal RMS is associated with loss of heterozygosity at 11p15.5 or gains on chromosome
8.
Alveolar RMS, in 70% to 80% of patients, is associated with a t(2;13) (q35;q14) translocation
associated with a FOXO1-PAX3 fusion and t(1;13) (p36;q14) translocation associated with a
FOXO1-PAX7 fusion. These can be detected via fluorescence in situ hybridization or reverse
transcriptase polymerase chain reaction techniques.
Spindle cell RMS in infants frequently is associated with mutations involving VGLL2 or NCOA2
fusions. Some older children and adults with spindle cell RMS have a specific MYOD1 (pL122R)
mutation that portends a more aggressive subtype with poorer prognosis.21 Approximately
50% of patients also may have activating PIK3CA mutations.
Predisposing factors include Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Ras-MAPkinase pathway disorders
(neurofibromatosis type 1 [NF1], Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome) in approximately one-
third of patients with RMS, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, DICER1 syndrome, and PIK3CA
mutations. Large birth weight and large for gestational age infants may have embryonal
RMS.22
Patient Age
Embryonal RMS has a peak in individuals aged 0 to 4 years, whereas alveolar RMS more
frequently is observed in adolescents and young adults. Pleomorphic RMS often is observed in

Sites
The genitourinary system, head and neck, and extremities are more commonly involved.
Alveolar RMS tends to more frequently involve the extremities. Hand and foot involvement is
observed in older patients, and alveolar histology is more frequent.
Clinical Features
Patient age and tumor location depend on the histologic subtype.
Patients often present with a painless soft-tissue mass.
Botryoid RMS presents as an exophytic bunch of grapes growth from epithelial lined mucosal
surfaces.
Imaging Studies
Imaging studies are fairly nonspecific, and tumors typically present as deep soft-tissue masses,
with a hypointense signal observed on T1-weighted MRIs and a hyperintense signal observed
on T2-weighted MRIs with heterogeneous contrast enhancement.
Imaging studies are essential for appropriate staging.
Staging Workup
Staging includes appropriate imaging before biopsy. Local extent can be evaluated via MRI or
CT.
Regional spread to lymph nodes is best appreciated via cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI)
followed by lymph node sampling, preferably via sentinel lymph node biopsy. This is required
for enrollment in COG studies for patients with extremity and trunk and paratesticular (age, 10
years or older) RMS, even with normal-appearing nodes on imaging studies. Distant spread is
assessed via chest CT in all patients with RMS. CT of the abdomen and pelvis is recommended
in patients with primary tumors of the trunk, extremity, and paratesticular region.
Bilateral bone marrow biopsy and full-body bone scintigraphy are recommended in all patients
except those with localized negative regional lymph nodes, noninvasive embryonal tumors,
and group I alveolar tumors.
PET is recommended for staging of RMS for evaluation of locoregional and distant spread.

Pathology
Embryonal RMS (60% to 70%) is the most common histologic subtype and incudes the botryoid
subtype (occurring on mucosal surfaces). Histologically, these are moderately cellular with
hypocellular and hypercellular areas separated by a loose myxoid stroma. The cells are small,
stellate, spindled, or round with eosinophilic cytoplasm and small eccentric flat nuclei.
Approximately 13% of patients with embryonal RMS have anaplastic features that may
influence outcome. Embryonal RMS with anaplastic features also may be a presenting feature
of TP53 mutation–associated RMS.
Alveolar RMS accounts for approximately 30% of RMS. It is more frequently observed in
adolescents and in the extremities, trunk, and perineal/perianal locations. The cells are larger
than embryonal RMS cells and poorly differentiated. The cellular areas are separated by
fibrous septa mimicking alveolar structure. Multinucleated giant cells often are observed.
Spindle cell RMS is an uncommon variant more often observed in paratesticular locations.
Pleomorphic RMS involves a mix of different cell types.
Immunohistochemistry shows desmin (nonspecific), and nuclear staining with myogenin and
MyoD1 (more specific) are essential to confirm a diagnosis of RMS. Alveolar RMS usually is
associated with more diffuse and strong staining with MyoD1 and myoglobin, whereas this
may be much more focal in embryonal RMS.
Management
Surgical Management
Management of the primary site usually is surgical unless resection causes considerable
morbidity.
Surgical management can be performed before starting chemotherapy; however, in patients
with an unresectable tumor or in whom morbidity from surgical treatment is very high,
delayed resection (postchemotherapy) may be performed.
Additional management can then be determined based on the extent of resection
(clinical/surgicopathologic grouping), the histology, and the primary site.
Tumor bed excision/primary re-resection may be performed if not associated with major
morbidity and may confer survival benefit if all residual microscopic tumor is resected. Gross
total resection confers the benefit of radiation therapy dose reduction.
Debulking surgery is not recommended because it does not result in any benefit over biopsy
alone.

All patients with RMS require chemotherapy.
Chemotherapy may be a combination of vincristine, dactinomycin, and cyclophosphamide.
Other agents used in different situations include doxorubicin, ifosfamide, irinotecan, and

Chemotherapy regimens are based on the group and risk stratification.
A detailed discussion of the various chemotherapeutic regimens is beyond the scope of this

Prognosis
The 5-year overall survival rate in children younger than 15 years and children aged 15 to 19
years is 67% and 51%, respectively.23 The low-risk group has approximately a 90% 5-year
survival rate; however, patients with metastatic disease have approximately a 20% to 30% 5-
year survival rate.
Prognostic factors include the following:
Patients aged 1 to 9 years have the best prognosis.
Site of origin plays a role in survival. Five-year survival is the best in patients with
genitourinary primary tumors (89%), followed by head and neck tumors (83%) and extremity
tumors (67%).
Patients with larger tumors (>5 cm) have a poorer prognosis; however, this is not a reliable
number in infants. Tumor volume and maximum tumor diameter also are related to
prognosis.

Imaging characteristics of NRSTS rarely are specific.
Radiographs may demonstrate mineralization in some patients (eg, synovial sarcoma).

Introduction
Synovial sarcoma is the second most common STS in children and young adults.
Its cell or origin is unknown.
It is an aggressive malignancy with a propensity for the extremities but can be observed in the
chest and many other sites.29
Patient Age
Adolescents and young adults account for approximately 20% of synovial sarcomas; the
remaining are observed in the adult population.
Site
Synovia sarcoma frequently occurs close to joints; however, the term is a misnomer because
the cell of origin is not a synovial cell, and a joint is involved in a minority of patients (0.5% to
5%).
Location is periarticular in most patients, with lower extremity involvement (especially the
knee and the ankle) more common than upper extremity involvement.
Most common sites are about the knee, ankle, and hip.
Synovial sarcoma is the most common STS of the foot and ankle in young adults.

Characteristic t(X;18) (p11;q11) translocation with fusion of S18-SSX family observed.

Observed in adolescents and young adults, this tumor may be mildly/minimally symptomatic
for a variable period.

The three most common histologic subtypes include monophasic, biphasic, and poorly

Introduction/Patient Age
Infantile fibrosarcoma (IFS) is the most common STS in children younger than 1 year.
IFS can be observed as early as birth (congenital IFS), with most (60%) patients diagnosed

IFS is characterized by a t(12;15) (p13;q25) translocation, with ETV6-NTRK3 gene fusion in most

IFS usually presents as a rapidly growing mass in the deep soft tissues of the extremities or

The behavior of IFS is less aggressive than the childhood counterpart, and some patients have
been documented to regress spontaneously.

On imaging studies, the tumor may appear isointense to hypointense on T1-weighted MRIs
and hyperintense on T2-weighted MRIs.
Restricted diffusion may be observed.

Histologically, IFS is a low-grade, densely cellular spindle cell neoplasm arranged in a

Limb Salvage Surgery
Limb salvage surgery is possible in approximately 80% to 85% patients with a malignant
bone tumor. The goal is adequate/wide tumor resection with preservation of function of
the residual limb. Several options are available for reconstructing the skeletal defect
after tumor resection. These alternatives can be divided into biologic solutions (bone
grafting, bone transport, van Nes rotationplasty) or endoprosthetic solutions. In
addition, surgical management of sarcoma in children may provide a physeal-sparing
solution, joint-sparing solution, or limb-sparing solution.
Vascularized Autograft
The most commonly treatment option is a vascularized fibular graft, either by itself or placed
within an allograft (Capanna technique).
Advantages include faster healing, quicker hypertrophy and resumption of load bearing, and
successful use in beds with compromised vascularity.
Disadvantages include size limitations, fracture risk, longer surgical times, and donor site
morbidity (ankle valgus and compromised extensor hallucis longus function).
Allograft
Bulk allografts can be used in various fashions to reconstruct skeletal defects. These include
osteoarticular allografts, intercalary allografts, allograft arthrodeses, and alloprosthetic
composite.
Osteoarticular allografts are associated with the advantage of preserving the nonaffected side
of the joint; however, given the cartilage degeneration and joint instability that may be

The infection risk is highest within the first year, and fracture risk is quite high until
approximately 3 years after implantation.
The advantages of allograft include that the biologic, restored bone stock can preserve soft-
tissue attachments and preserve the uninvolved side of the joint in osteoarticular applications.
The disadvantages of allograft include a high complication rate, usually within the first 3 years,
the need for restricted mobilization and weight bearing postoperatively until union is achieved,
increased risk for infection, and mechanical failure rate compared with endoprostheses.
Therefore, allografts are being used in more limited applications compared with
endoprosthetic reconstruction.
Endoprosthetic Reconstruction
With current improvements in technology and metallurgy, the use of endoprosthetic
reconstruction has expanded in the past several years.
Advantages of endoprosthetic reconstruction include modularity, low risk of infection and
fracture compared with allografts, no risk of disease transmission and immunologic response,
and early weight bearing and mobilization of the affected extremity.
Disadvantages of endoprosthetic reconstruction include polyethylene wear, aseptic loosening,
a somewhat high risk of infection (10% to 15%), soft-tissue failure, mechanical failure, and
limited options in certain anatomic locations.31

Expandable endoprostheses are one of the possible reconstruction methods for children
undergoing limb salvage surgery if resection of the tumor will result in considerable (at least 3
cm) anticipated limb-length discrepancy at maturity.
The age range for the use of expandable endoprostheses is approximately 7 to 10 years
because the bone must be of adequate size to allow for implantation of the expandable
endoprostheses.
Many surgeons avoid using expandable endoprostheses in patients with metastatic disease or
in whom poor survival is anticipated.
The hardware available for expandable endoprostheses has evolved, with noninvasive
expansion recently becoming more popular.
Expandable endoprostheses are not without challenges and are associated with a high
complication rate (approximately 40% to 45%) and the need for revision surgery.
Deep infection is the most common mode for failure of expandable endoprostheses.
Rotationplasty
Rotationplasty is an intercalary amputation with resection of the tumor and rotation of the
distal segment 180° and shortening the limb, such that the ankle functions as the new knee
and the foot functions as the below-knee component of the residual limb.
Rotationplasty typically is performed if muscle left over from resection is inadequate to power
the extremity via a standard reconstructive option.
Rotationplasty also may be performed as a salvage procedure after failed limb salvage (eg,
infected endoprosthesis).
Winkelmann32 classified rotationplasty based on whether the native hip can be preserved
(type A, better functional results) or not (type B).
An essential prerequisite is a functioning sciatic nerve and muscles to power the foot.
The advantage of a rotationplasty is a lower level of energy consumption compared with an
above-knee amputation and a higher level of activity and sports activity compared with
patients with an above-knee amputation.
The biggest challenge is the appearance and psychological acceptance of the residual limb.

Malignant bone and STS in children are less common than their benign counterparts.
Often, STS have a nonspecific appearance on imaging studies, and a biopsy is necessary
to establish a diagnosis. Chemotherapy has played an important role in improving the
prognosis of bone sarcomas. Surgical management is the preferred form of local control
in bone and STS if feasible. Limb salvage surgery is feasible in most patients with bone or
STS. With improvements in metallurgy, metal endoprostheses are being used more
frequently than allografts. No considerable difference in oncologic outcomes has been
observed in patients undergoing limb salvage versus amputation.
